report.headline: Usage rate projected to fall to 14.4% in the NBA, well below league average, while the shooting efficiency model fails a basic reliability check.

projection.text: Usage rate is projected at 14.4% in the NBA, down from 18.2% in the 2016-17 EuroLeague season and well below the NBA's minutes-weighted average of 20.1% (SD 5.2%).

risks.text: The true-shooting projection is unreliable: the model's out-of-fold error (4.7%) is identical to that of the trivial league-mean baseline (4.7%) over 367 held-out transitions.
Projected usage rate of 14.4% sits more than a full standard deviation below the NBA average of 20.1% (SD 5.2%), pointing to a much smaller offensive role than in the EuroLeague.
Took only 0.4% of shot attempts from three in the source season, raising doubts about fit as a floor-spacer in the NBA.
The projection rests on a thin, older-player sample: 993 minutes over 31 games at age 29.0.

strengths.text: Posted a true shooting percentage of 60.9% in the source season, 0.60 standard deviations above the EuroLeague average.
Combined 8.738 rebounds per 75 possessions with 13.633 points per 75 possessions in the source season.
Kept turnovers low (11.0% turnover rate) while posting a 13.0% assist rate in a modest offensive role.
Belongs to a cohort of EL->NBA movers who already stood 0.46 standard deviations above their own league's average, consistent with selection for above-average skill.

uncertainty.text: The usage-rate model (3.3% MAE) modestly beats the league-mean baseline (4.3% MAE), but its 80% interval of 9.1%-19.6% still spans roughly two standard deviations of NBA usage (SD 5.2%), so it can rank but not pin down an individual value. The true-shooting model (4.7% MAE) is no better than simply predicting the league mean (4.7% MAE), so its projection carries no information and should not be used.
